subject: Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
parts:
Does anyone know of any literature on priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable? Here's what I have in mind:
  • You have an ordinal input variable x[N] with K levels.
  • You have K (or K-1) corresponding effects betax[K].
  • You must have betax[k+1] > betax[k].
  • The linear predictor for observation i includes a term betax[x[i]].
I don't want to have to assume that the betax values are equally spaced, but it would be good if the prior could penalize very small differences between beta[k] and beta[k+1].

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
parts:
This has been discussed before, albeit inconclusively.

Yes, that's one way to do it. I've been asking Andrew about this
for a while and he didn't have a recommendation (or if he did, maybe
he can remind us all).

To construct a sequence of cutpoints, you can fix the first
at 0 and then define

c[1] <- 0;
c[n+1] = c[n] + delta[n]

where delta[n] has to be positive. You can define

delta_raw ~ normal(0, 2);

or another unconstrained prior and then take

delta <- exp(delta_raw);

or you can constrain the delta to be positive and put any prior
on them. Like a lognormal or gamma.

Or you can just model all the cutpoints as having independent
priors, which gives you the same result as generating them
independently and sorting given the constraint (I've verified this
all computationally but haven't quite got my head around why it's
true theoretically --- there are lots of moving boundaries to adjust
for).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Priors for the regression coefficients of an ordinal input variable
parts:
Anyone care to comment on this possible prior for the effects of a K-level ordinal input variable? The idea is that you use a Dirichlet distribution for partitioning the range from beta[1] to beta[K], and you use an independent prior on the magnitude of that range.

    beta[1] <- -scale;
    beta[K] <- scale;
    // Now make beta[k + 1] - beta[k] be fraction p[k] of (beta[K] - beta[1])
    range <- beta[K] - beta[1];
    b <- beta[1];
    for (k = 1; k + 1 < K; ++k)
        beta[k + 1] <- beta[k] + p[k] * range;
    
    scale ~ normal(0, sigma);
    p ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(alpha, K-1));

Larger values for alpha give a larger preference for equally-spaced betas.

parts:
Looks like nobody responded.

I think scaling a Dirichlet draw makes sense if you want to put
a prior that favors even distribution of segments. I don't have
any intuition at all about how these problems work.

You have to be careful about what's getting sampled. I wasn't
sure where that was in what you did. This would work, with a
lower bound, width, and simplex parameters, combined into a
vector c of cutpoints.

parameters {
real low;
real width;
simplex[K - 1] theta;
}
transformed parameters {
ordered[K] c;
c[0] <- low;
for (i in 2:K)
c[i] <- c[i - 1] + width * theta[k];
}
model {
theta ~ dirichlet(rep(alpha, K - 1));
low ~ ???
width ~ ???

Why did you center yours on zero? I'm also not sure about what
to do with the lower bound. You need to make sure not to have
too many degress of freedom --- maybe the lower bound needs to
be fixed at theta?

I find it easier working directly in terms of a width parameter
rather than a half-width, but a lot of this is just personal preference.

- Bob
